NO reference disclosed these elements. They are the strongest ground the independent claims have, so build on them rather than adding new limitations:
  - single-hand portable design with all components carried by rigid body without external hose or cord
  - warning threshold defined relative to load-release vacuum rather than working vacuum

Do this:
  1. Read every newly attached reference in prior_art/ before changing anything.
  2. Amend the independent claims so each recites, in its own terms, at least one concrete feature or relationship that NO attached reference discloses, and that does real technical work. Prefer a feature the search already showed nothing disclosed.
  3. Make sure the detailed description supports that feature in the same words, and explain the technical problem it solves, because that explanation is what a later argument is built from.
  4. Address the new references accurately in the Background.

DO NOT buy a lower score with scope. Narrowing claim 1 until nothing reads on it is always available and is almost always the wrong trade: add the distinguishing feature the disclosure supports, do not pile on limitations. If the honest answer is that the art is close and the disclosure supports no further distinction, say so plainly in your reasoning and leave the claim alone.

1	A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is used to move glass panes, stone slabs, and similar flat panels on site by suction gripping. A suction cup is pressed against the face of the panel, air is removed from the space enclosed between the cup and the panel, and the resulting difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in that enclosed space clamps the cup to the panel so that the panel can be carried.
2	
3	A suction grip is only as good as its seal. Dust on the panel, a textured or porous surface, a nick in the sealing lip, a change in temperature, or simply the slow permeation and leakage that occurs over minutes of handling will all bleed air back into the enclosed space. As air returns, the clamping force falls. The failure is progressive and, from the point of view of the person holding the panel, silent: nothing about the feel of the tool changes until the cup lets go, at which point a heavy panel is already falling.
4	
5	Vacuum lifting equipment has therefore long been fitted with vacuum monitoring. In one known lifter for transporting loads having an adhesion surface, a suction plate assembly carries projecting annular seals defining a vacuum chamber connected to a main vacuum source, a battery-fed emergency vacuum source that can be started by an emergency switch is additionally provided, and a pressure pickup associated with the vacuum chamber is coupled with a malfunction alarm such that the alarm is turned on when a preset limit pressure is exceeded during vacuum operation [REF:US-5310232-A]. That equipment is a suspended plate assembly with a main vacuum source and a separate emergency vacuum source; the alarm is described as a malfunction alarm tied to a preset limit pressure, and the reference does not describe the limit pressure in terms of the vacuum still needed to keep hold of the load.
6	
7	Control systems for vacuum lift equipment have also been described in which a programmable controller interprets feedback from vacuum level sensors and battery sensors and responsively provides warnings and limits or alters machine functions, including evaluating a change in measured vacuum level over time to determine a rate of vacuum level change that may be caused by a leak and outputting a warning indication when that rate exceeds a threshold rate [REF:US-10518985-B2]. Such a system is built around a controller with memory, stored records, and machine-function interlocks, and its leak warning is a response to how fast the vacuum is changing rather than to where the vacuum sits relative to the point at which the grip would fail.
8	
9	Powered suction devices in a hand-carried format are also known. An electric vacuum suction lifter has been described having a main body with a suction surface carrying first and second annular sealing units that bound a sealed space, a control unit, a vacuum pump controlled by the control unit to draw air from the sealed space, a pressure sensing unit that measures the pressure of the sealed space to generate instant pressure information, a battery unit that is charged by external power equipment and powers the control unit, pump, and pressure sensing unit, a start button, a pressure relief button, and at least one handle by which a member gripped by the device can be carried [REF:US-10625955-B2]. In that device the instant pressure information is compared with a high predetermined pressure and a low predetermined pressure: reaching the high predetermined pressure stops the pump, and falling below the low predetermined pressure restarts the pump. A warning unit is described as being operated when the detected battery power is below a predetermined battery power, and warning information relating to pressure is described as being transmitted to an external electronic device. A closely similar electric suction cup has likewise been described, in which the pressure detection unit detects the pressure between the suction cup and the component in real time and the vacuum pump automatically acts again when that pressure is lower than a second predetermined pressure [REF:CN-110630621-B].
10	
11	Hand-carried suction devices that signal something about their own state are also known. A sucker for plate glass has been described having a sucker body defining a suction hole at a suction surface, a manually operatable vacuum pump carried on the body, a sensor communicating with the suction channel that connects the suction hole at the suction surface with the suction hole in the pump, and a sound generator that is turned on through a switch closed by the sensor when the degree of vacuum sensed reaches a predetermined value [REF:US-5184858-A]. The pump in that device is worked by hand rather than electrically, and the sound is generated at a predetermined degree of vacuum which the reference does not relate to the vacuum still needed to retain the sheet.
12	
13	A portable hand grab has been described including one or more suction cups, at least one handle connected to the suction cups for gripping by hand, at least one electrical vacuum pump for at least partially evacuating the suction volume between the suction cups and the attachment surfaces, at least one vacuum sensor for detecting a vacuum level in the suction volume, and an electronic controller configured to control the pump to at least partially evacuate the suction volume when the vacuum sensor detects the vacuum level being less than a preselected minimum vacuum level, optionally together with an attach indicator that the controller activates when the vacuum sensor detects the vacuum level being greater than a preselected safe vacuum level [REF:WO-2017156581-A1]. The signal there tells the user that the vacuum is high enough to attach, and a vacuum below the preselected minimum vacuum level is answered by running the pump again rather than by telling the user that the grip is going.
14	
15	A cordless wand device for grasping objects such as silicon wafers has been described having a housing with a hollow interior, a tip attached to the housing through a hollow tube and having a perimeter region contoured to form an airtight seal against the object, a power source and a vacuum pump positioned within the housing, and light-emitting diodes of different colours which indicate to an operator whether the power source is sufficiently charged to generate sufficient suction force to safely grasp the object, that sufficiency being determined from the voltage drop across resistors connected across the power source [REF:US-5374090-A]. What is indicated in that device is the state of the power source rather than the state of the grip on the object.
16	
17	A portable electric carrying suction cup structure has been described in which a handle is fixed on the upper end of the suction cup body, a vacuum pump is provided on the suction cup body, and a control unit is connected between the power supply part and the vacuum pump, so that air continues to be pumped out after the suction cup body and the material surface have reached an airtight state; the control unit is provided with a pressure gauge by which the user can know the pressure change between the suction cup body and the surface, with a light source for displaying different usage states, and with a buzzer for sending out alarm sounds according to different usage states [REF:CN-2806399-Y]. That reference attributes the avoidance of loosening and falling during movement to the continued pumping, and it describes the buzzer as sounding according to different usage states without relating any sounding condition to the vacuum at which the cup would let go of the material.
18	
19	A digital display suction cup has been described comprising a suction cup and a handle structure, the two ends of the handle structure being provided with a switch button and a pressure relief valve, the handle structure being provided with a battery and a vacuum electric pump which is connected to the suction cup through an air pipe, with an air pressure sensor and a display screen at the lower part of the battery end, a USB charging port electrically connected to the battery, and an inner side of the suction cup provided with an evacuation hole, a pressure relief hole, and a sensing through hole [REF:US-2024424646-A1]. That device monitors and maintains negative pressure in real time and shows the negative pressure value and the battery power on the display screen as numbers for the user to read.
20	
21	Multi-cup handling equipment has been described in which two or more vacuum modules are mounted on a mounting frame, each module having a cup, an electrically powered vacuum pump, a fluid circuit, a controller, and optionally a pressure sensor and a battery, with an interface through which a user selects an operational mode of the modules, and in which each module may include indicators that indicate a functional condition of the module visually or audibly [REF:WO-2022236379-A1].
22	
23	Three shortcomings persist for a person who is holding a panel in one hand. First, the response to a decaying grip in the known powered devices is to run the pump again: the device treats a falling vacuum as a housekeeping event to be corrected, and the low pressure value at which it acts is chosen with reference to the working vacuum, not with reference to how much grip is left. If the leak is larger than the pump can make up - a torn lip, a dusty or porous panel, a cracked substrate - the pump simply runs while the grip continues to decay, and the user is told nothing until the panel is gone. Second, where a signal is given, it is given on a condition unrelated to grip (battery state), on a rate of change, on a preset limit whose relationship to the load-holding capacity of the cup is not established, as a confirmation that the vacuum is high enough to attach, or as a number on a display which the user must look at and interpret while carrying a panel. None of these delivers the one thing a person carrying a slab actually needs: notice that arrives while the cup is still holding, with grip left over to get the panel down.
24	
25	Third, the equipment that has the most elaborate response to a failing grip is the equipment that is not carried in the hand. A suspended plate assembly can be provided with a battery-fed emergency vacuum source that an emergency switch starts [REF:US-5310232-A], and a controller for vacuum lift equipment can limit or alter machine functions in response to sensor feedback [REF:US-10518985-B2]. A lifter that is carried in the hand has none of those remedies available to it: the only thing that can act on a failing grip is the person holding the handle, and that person can only act if the notice arrives early enough.
26	
27	There remains a need for a cordless handheld vacuum lifter that tells the user that the grip is failing while the cup is still holding, so that the warning arrives before the load can be dropped.
28

1	This summary introduces a selection of concepts that are described further in the detailed description. It is not intended to identify essential features of the claimed subject matter, nor to limit the scope of the claims.
2	
3	A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is disclosed. The lifter has a rigid body comprising a handle, and a suction cup carried by the rigid body. The suction cup comprises a flexible sealing lip. An electric vacuum pump is disposed within the rigid body and draws air through a port to create a grip vacuum, the grip vacuum retaining a load on the suction cup. A pressure sensor monitors the grip vacuum. A warning indicator is driven by the pressure sensor. A rechargeable battery powers the electric vacuum pump.
4	
5	The grip vacuum is treated throughout this disclosure as a positive magnitude: it is the amount by which the pressure between the suction cup and the load is below the ambient pressure outside the lifter, so that a larger grip vacuum means a firmer grip and a decaying grip is a falling grip vacuum.
6	
7	The warning indicator activates when the grip vacuum is lost, and is configured to activate before the load can be dropped.
8	
9	Because the rechargeable battery powers the electric vacuum pump, the lifter grips, monitors, and warns without a cord to an external power supply.
10	
11	A method of lifting a glass or stone panel with such a lifter is also disclosed. The method includes placing the flexible sealing lip against the panel, drawing air through the port with the electric vacuum pump powered by the rechargeable battery to create the grip vacuum, lifting and carrying the panel by the handle, monitoring the grip vacuum with the pressure sensor while the panel is retained on the suction cup, and activating the warning indicator upon loss of the grip vacuum, before the panel can be dropped.

This summary introduces a selection of concepts that are described further in the detailed description. It is not intended to identify essential features of the claimed subject matter, nor to limit the scope of the claims.

A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is disclosed. The lifter has a rigid body comprising a handle, and a suction cup carried by the rigid body. The suction cup comprises a flexible sealing lip. An electric vacuum pump is disposed within the rigid body and draws air through a port to create a grip vacuum, the grip vacuum retaining a load on the suction cup. A pressure sensor monitors the grip vacuum. A warning indicator is driven by the pressure sensor. A rechargeable battery powers the electric vacuum pump.

The grip vacuum is treated throughout this disclosure as a positive magnitude: it is the amount by which the pressure between the suction cup and the load is below the ambient pressure outside the lifter, so that a larger grip vacuum means a firmer grip and a decaying grip is a falling grip vacuum.

The warning indicator activates when the grip vacuum is lost, and is configured to activate before the load can be dropped.

Because the rechargeable battery powers the electric vacuum pump, the lifter grips, monitors, and warns without a cord to an external power supply.

A method of lifting a glass or stone panel with such a lifter is also disclosed. The method includes placing the flexible sealing lip against the panel, drawing air through the port with the electric vacuum pump powered by the rechargeable battery to create the grip vacuum, lifting and carrying the panel by the handle, monitoring the grip vacuum with the pressure sensor while the panel is retained on the suction cup, and activating the warning indicator upon loss of the grip vacuum, before the panel can be dropped.

1	In the following description, reference is made to the accompanying drawings, which form a part hereof and in which are shown by way of illustration specific embodiments. Other embodiments may be used and structural changes may be made without departing from the scope of the disclosure. Like numerals refer to like parts throughout.
2	
3	Terminology used in this disclosure has the following meanings. The grip vacuum is the vacuum created when an electric vacuum pump 20 of the cordless handheld vacuum lifter draws air through a port 22, expressed as a positive magnitude: it is the amount by which the pressure between the suction cup 10 and the load is below the ambient atmospheric pressure surrounding the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100. A grip vacuum of zero corresponds to no grip at all; the grip vacuum rises as the electric vacuum pump 20 draws air away and falls as the grip decays.
4	
5	FIG. 1 shows a cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 comprises a rigid body 14 comprising a handle 16, and a suction cup 10 carried by the rigid body 14. The suction cup 10 comprises a flexible sealing lip 12. In use, the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against a panel 50 of glass or stone, and the panel 50 is the load which the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 carries. The electric vacuum pump 20, being disposed within the rigid body 14, is shown in broken lines in FIG. 1.
6	
7	FIG. 2 shows schematically the suction cup 10, the port 22, the electric vacuum pump 20, a pressure sensor 30, a warning indicator 32, and a rechargeable battery 40, and the connections among them.
8	
9	The electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14 and is configured to draw air through the port 22 to create a grip vacuum, by which grip vacuum the suction cup 10 retains the load. The pressure sensor 30 is configured to monitor the grip vacuum. The warning indicator 32 is driven by the pressure sensor 30. The rechargeable battery 40 is configured to power the electric vacuum pump 20.
10	
11	The warning indicator 32 activates when the grip vacuum is lost, and is configured to activate before the load can be dropped.
12	
13	The rechargeable battery 40 powers the electric vacuum pump 20, so that the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 grips, monitors the grip vacuum, and warns without a cord to an external power supply, including while the panel 50 is carried.
14	
15	The panel 50 is a glass or stone panel, and the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against a face of the panel 50 when the panel 50 is to be lifted.
16	
17	FIG. 3 is a flow diagram of a method of lifting a panel with the cordless handheld vacuum lifter, the method comprising a placing step 202, an evacuating step 204, a lifting step 205, a monitoring step 206, and an activating step 208.
18	
19	At the placing step 202, the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against the panel 50. At the evacuating step 204, the electric vacuum pump 20, powered by the rechargeable battery 40, draws air through the port 22 and creates the grip vacuum. At the lifting step 205, the panel 50 is lifted and carried by the handle 16, the panel 50 being retained on the suction cup 10 by the grip vacuum. At the monitoring step 206, the pressure sensor 30 monitors the grip vacuum while the panel 50 is retained on the suction cup 10. At the activating step 208, upon loss of the grip vacuum, the pressure sensor 30 drives the warning indicator 32 to activate. The activating step 208 occurs before the panel 50 can be dropped.
20	
21	The embodiments described above are illustrative rather than limiting. Features described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another unless the combination is technically impossible. The scope of protection is defined by the claims.

Terminology used in this disclosure has the following meanings. The grip vacuum is the vacuum created when an electric vacuum pump 20 of the cordless handheld vacuum lifter draws air through a port 22, expressed as a positive magnitude: it is the amount by which the pressure between the suction cup 10 and the load is below the ambient atmospheric pressure surrounding the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100. A grip vacuum of zero corresponds to no grip at all; the grip vacuum rises as the electric vacuum pump 20 draws air away and falls as the grip decays.

FIG. 1 shows a cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 comprises a rigid body 14 comprising a handle 16, and a suction cup 10 carried by the rigid body 14. The suction cup 10 comprises a flexible sealing lip 12. In use, the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against a panel 50 of glass or stone, and the panel 50 is the load which the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 carries. The electric vacuum pump 20, being disposed within the rigid body 14, is shown in broken lines in FIG. 1.

FIG. 2 shows schematically the suction cup 10, the port 22, the electric vacuum pump 20, a pressure sensor 30, a warning indicator 32, and a rechargeable battery 40, and the connections among them.

The electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14 and is configured to draw air through the port 22 to create a grip vacuum, by which grip vacuum the suction cup 10 retains the load. The pressure sensor 30 is configured to monitor the grip vacuum. The warning indicator 32 is driven by the pressure sensor 30. The rechargeable battery 40 is configured to power the electric vacuum pump 20.

The warning indicator 32 activates when the grip vacuum is lost, and is configured to activate before the load can be dropped.

The rechargeable battery 40 powers the electric vacuum pump 20, so that the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 grips, monitors the grip vacuum, and warns without a cord to an external power supply, including while the panel 50 is carried.

The panel 50 is a glass or stone panel, and the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against a face of the panel 50 when the panel 50 is to be lifted.

FIG. 3 is a flow diagram of a method of lifting a panel with the cordless handheld vacuum lifter, the method comprising a placing step 202, an evacuating step 204, a lifting step 205, a monitoring step 206, and an activating step 208.

At the placing step 202, the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against the panel 50. At the evacuating step 204, the electric vacuum pump 20, powered by the rechargeable battery 40, draws air through the port 22 and creates the grip vacuum. At the lifting step 205, the panel 50 is lifted and carried by the handle 16, the panel 50 being retained on the suction cup 10 by the grip vacuum. At the monitoring step 206, the pressure sensor 30 monitors the grip vacuum while the panel 50 is retained on the suction cup 10. At the activating step 208, upon loss of the grip vacuum, the pressure sensor 30 drives the warning indicator 32 to activate. The activating step 208 occurs before the panel 50 can be dropped.

The embodiments described above are illustrative rather than limiting. Features described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another unless the combination is technically impossible. The scope of protection is defined by the claims.

Abstract: An electric sucker comprises a body, a vacuum pump, a pressure sensing unit and a start key. content.content:
1	A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is used to move glass panes, stone slabs, and similar flat panels on site by suction gripping. A suction cup is pressed against the face of the panel, air is removed from the space enclosed between the cup and the panel, and the resulting difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in that enclosed space clamps the cup to the panel so that the panel can be carried.
2	
3	A suction grip is only as good as its seal. Dust on the panel, a textured or porous surface, a nick in the sealing lip, a change in temperature, or simply the slow permeation and leakage that occurs over minutes of handling will all bleed air back into the enclosed space. As air returns, the clamping force falls. The failure is progressive and, from the point of view of the person holding the panel, silent: nothing about the feel of the tool changes until the cup lets go, at which point a heavy panel is already falling.
4	
5	Vacuum lifting equipment has therefore long been fitted with vacuum monitoring. In one known lifter for transporting loads having an adhesion surface, a suction plate assembly carries projecting annular seals defining a vacuum chamber connected to a main vacuum source, a battery-fed emergency vacuum source that can be started by an emergency switch is additionally provided, and a pressure pickup associated with the vacuum chamber is coupled with a malfunction alarm such that the alarm is turned on when a preset limit pressure is exceeded during vacuum operation [REF:US-5310232-A]. That equipment is a suspended plate assembly with a main vacuum source and a separate emergency vacuum source; the alarm is described as a malfunction alarm tied to a preset limit pressure, and the reference does not describe the limit pressure in terms of the vacuum still needed to keep hold of the load.
6	
7	Control systems for vacuum lift equipment have also been described in which a programmable controller interprets feedback from vacuum level sensors and battery sensors and responsively provides warnings and limits or alters machine functions, including evaluating a change in measured vacuum level over time to determine a rate of vacuum level change that may be caused by a leak and outputting a warning indication when that rate exceeds a threshold rate [REF:US-10518985-B2]. Such a system is built around a controller with memory, stored records, and machine-function interlocks, and its leak warning is a response to how fast the vacuum is changing rather than to where the vacuum sits relative to the point at which the grip would fail.
8	
9	Powered suction devices in a hand-carried format are also known. An electric vacuum suction lifter has been described having a main body with a suction surface carrying first and second annular sealing units that bound a sealed space, a control unit, a vacuum pump controlled by the control unit to draw air from the sealed space, a pressure sensing unit that measures the pressure of the sealed space to generate instant pressure information, a battery unit that is charged by external power equipment and powers the control unit, pump, and pressure sensing unit, a start button, a pressure relief button, and at least one handle by which a member gripped by the device can be carried [REF:US-10625955-B2]. In that device the instant pressure information is compared with a high predetermined pressure and a low predetermined pressure: reaching the high predetermined pressure stops the pump, and falling below the low predetermined pressure restarts the pump. A warning unit is described as being operated when the detected battery power is below a predetermined battery power, and warning information relating to pressure is described as being transmitted to an external electronic device. A closely similar electric suction cup has likewise been described, in which the pressure detection unit detects the pressure between the suction cup and the component in real time and the vacuum pump automatically acts again when that pressure is lower than a second predetermined pressure [REF:CN-110630621-B].
10	
11	Hand-carried suction devices that signal something about their own state are also known. A sucker for plate glass has been described having a sucker body defining a suction hole at a suction surface, a manually operatable vacuum pump carried on the body, a sensor communicating with the suction channel that connects the suction hole at the suction surface with the suction hole in the pump, and a sound generator that is turned on through a switch closed by the sensor when the degree of vacuum sensed reaches a predetermined value [REF:US-5184858-A]. The pump in that device is worked by hand rather than electrically, and the sound is generated at a predetermined degree of vacuum which the reference does not relate to the vacuum still needed to retain the sheet.
12	
13	A portable hand grab has been described including one or more suction cups, at least one handle connected to the suction cups for gripping by hand, at least one electrical vacuum pump for at least partially evacuating the suction volume between the suction cups and the attachment surfaces, at least one vacuum sensor for detecting a vacuum level in the suction volume, and an electronic controller configured to control the pump to at least partially evacuate the suction volume when the vacuum sensor detects the vacuum level being less than a preselected minimum vacuum level, optionally together with an attach indicator that the controller activates when the vacuum sensor detects the vacuum level being greater than a preselected safe vacuum level [REF:WO-2017156581-A1]. 14	
15	A cordless wand device for grasping objects such as silicon wafers has been described having a housing with a hollow interior, a tip attached to the housing through a hollow tube and having a perimeter region contoured to form an airtight seal against the object, a power source and a vacuum pump positioned within the housing, and light-emitting diodes of different colours which indicate to an operator whether the power source is sufficiently charged to generate sufficient suction force to safely grasp the object, that sufficiency being determined from the voltage drop across resistors connected across the power source [REF:US-5374090-A]. 16	
17	A portable electric carrying suction cup structure has been described in which a handle is fixed on the upper end of the suction cup body, a vacuum pump is provided on the suction cup body, and a control unit is connected between the power supply part and the vacuum pump, so that air continues to be pumped out after the suction cup body and the material surface have reached an airtight state; the control unit is provided with a pressure gauge by which the user can know the pressure change between the suction cup body and the surface, with a light source for displaying different usage states, and with a buzzer for sending out alarm sounds according to different usage states [REF:CN-2806399-Y]. That reference attributes the avoidance of loosening and falling during movement to the continued pumping, and it describes the buzzer as sounding according to different usage states without relating any sounding condition to the vacuum at which the cup would let go of the material.
18	
19	A digital display suction cup has been described comprising a suction cup and a handle structure, the two ends of the handle structure being provided with a switch button and a pressure relief valve, the handle structure being provided with a battery and a vacuum electric pump which is connected to the suction cup through an air pipe, with an air pressure sensor and a display screen at the lower part of the battery end, a USB charging port electrically connected to the battery, and an inner side of the suction cup provided with an evacuation hole, a pressure relief hole, and a sensing through hole [REF:US-2024424646-A1]. 20	
21	Multi-cup handling equipment has been described in which two or more vacuum modules are mounted on a mounting frame, each module having a cup, an electrically powered vacuum pump, a fluid circuit, a controller, and optionally a pressure sensor and a battery, with an interface through which a user selects an operational mode of the modules, and in which each module may include indicators that indicate a functional condition of the module visually or audibly [REF:WO-2022236379-A1].

23	Three shortcomings persist for a person who is holding a panel in one hand. First, the response to a decaying grip in the known powered devices is to run the pump again: the device treats a falling vacuum as a housekeeping event to be corrected, and the low pressure value at which it acts is chosen with reference to the working vacuum, not with reference to how much grip is left. If the leak is larger than the pump can make up - a torn lip, a dusty or porous panel, a cracked substrate - the pump simply runs while the grip continues to decay, and the user is told nothing until the panel is gone. Second, where a signal is given, it is given on a condition unrelated to grip (battery state), on a rate of change, on a preset limit whose relationship to the load-holding capacity of the cup is not established, as a confirmation that the vacuum is high enough to attach, or as a number on a display which the user must look at and interpret while carrying a panel. None of these delivers the one thing a person carrying a slab actually needs: notice that arrives while the cup is still holding, with grip left over to get the panel down.
24	
25	Third, the equipment that has the most elaborate response to a failing grip is the equipment that is not carried in the hand. A suspended plate assembly can be provided with a battery-fed emergency vacuum source that an emergency switch starts [REF:US-5310232-A], and a controller for vacuum lift equipment can limit or alter machine functions in response to sensor feedback [REF:US-10518985-B2]. A lifter that is carried in the hand has none of those remedies available to it: the only thing that can act on a failing grip is the person holding the handle, and that person can only act if the notice arrives early enough.
26	
27	There remains a need for a cordless handheld vacuum lifter that tells the user that the grip is failing while the cup is still holding, so that the warning arrives before the load can be dropped.

A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is used to move glass panes, stone slabs, and similar flat panels on site by suction gripping. A suction cup is pressed against the face of the panel, air is removed from the space enclosed between the cup and the panel, and the resulting difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in that enclosed space clamps the cup to the panel so that the panel can be carried.

A suction grip is only as good as its seal. Dust on the panel, a textured or porous surface, a nick in the sealing lip, a change in temperature, or simply the slow permeation and leakage that occurs over minutes of handling will all bleed air back into the enclosed space. As air returns, the clamping force falls. The failure is progressive and, from the point of view of the person holding the panel, silent: nothing about the feel of the tool changes until the cup lets go, at which point a heavy panel is already falling.

Abstract: An electric sucker comprises a body, a vacuum pump, a pressure sensing unit and a start key. When the user presses the activation key, the vacuum pump will act to pump out the air between the electric sucker and the component attached to the electric sucker, so that the electric sucker is adsorbed on the component. The pressure sensing unit can detect the pressure between the electric sucker and the component in real time. When the pressure sensing unit detects that the pressure between the electric suction cup and the component is lower than a second preset pressure, the vacuum pump automatically acts to pump out the air between the electric suction cup and the component again. After the user sets up the electric chuck on the component that wants to adsorb, can make the electric chuck adsorb automatically on simply through pressing the start key on the component. Then, the electric suction cup can automatically detect the pressure between the electric suction cup and the component in real time, and automatically perform air suction again when the pressure is lower than a second preset pressure, so that the safety of related personnel using the electric suction cup can be ensured.

A fluid circuit interconnects the vacuum pump with the port. The vacuum pump is operable to draw gas from within the internal region through the fluid circuit to generate a partial vacuum within the internal region and reversibly attach the cup to the workpiece. An interface is configured to communicate with controllers of the vacuum modules. A user selects an operational mode of the vacuum modules; the state of the controllers is dependent on the selected operational mode.

file.content: The present disclosure relates to cordless handheld vacuum lifters, and more particularly to a cordless handheld vacuum lifter having a grip-loss warning indicator.

content.content:
1	A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is used to move glass panes, stone slabs, and similar flat panels on site by suction gripping. A suction cup is pressed against the face of the panel, air is removed from the space enclosed between the cup and the panel, and the resulting difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in that enclosed space clamps the cup to the panel so that the panel can be carried.
2	
3	A suction grip is only as good as its seal. Dust on the panel, a textured or porous surface, a nick in the sealing lip, a change in temperature, or simply the slow permeation and leakage that occurs over minutes of handling will all bleed air back into the enclosed space. As air returns, the clamping force falls. The failure is progressive and, from the point of view of the person holding the panel, silent: nothing about the feel of the tool changes until the cup lets go, at which point a heavy panel is already falling.
4	
5	Vacuum lifting equipment has therefore long been fitted with vacuum monitoring. In one known lifter for transporting loads having an adhesion surface, a suction plate assembly carries projecting annular seals defining a vacuum chamber connected to a main vacuum source, a battery-fed emergency vacuum source that can be started by an emergency switch is additionally provided, and a pressure pickup associated with the vacuum chamber is coupled with a malfunction alarm such that the alarm is turned on when a preset limit pressure is exceeded during vacuum operation [REF:US-5310232-A]. That equipment is a suspended plate assembly with a main vacuum source and a separate emergency vacuum source; the alarm is described as a malfunction alarm tied to a preset limit pressure, and the reference does not describe the limit pressure in terms of the vacuum still needed to keep hold of the load.
6	
7	Control systems for vacuum lift equipment have also been described in which a programmable controller interprets feedback from vacuum level sensors and battery sensors and responsively provides warnings and limits or alters machine functions, including evaluating a change in measured vacuum level over time to determine a rate of vacuum level change that may be caused by a leak and outputting a warning indication when that rate exceeds a threshold rate [REF:US-10518985-B2]. Such a system is built around a controller with memory, stored records, and machine-function interlocks, and its leak warning is a response to how fast the vacuum is changing rather than to where the vacuum sits relative to the point at which the grip would fail.
8	
9	Powered suction devices in a hand-carried format are also known. An electric vacuum suction lifter has been described having a main body with a suction surface carrying first and second annular sealing units that bound a sealed space, a control unit, a vacuum pump controlled by the control unit to draw air from the sealed space, a pressure sensing unit that measures the pressure of the sealed space to generate instant pressure information, a battery unit that is charged by external power equipment and powers the control unit, pump, and pressure sensing unit, a start button, a pressure relief button, and at least one handle by which a member gripped by the device can be carried [REF:US-10625955-B2]. In that device the instant pressure information is compared with a high predetermined pressure and a low predetermined pressure: reaching the high predetermined pressure stops the pump, and falling below the low predetermined pressure restarts the pump. A warning unit is described as being operated when the detected battery power is below a predetermined battery power, and warning information relating to pressure is described as being transmitted to an external electronic device. A closely similar electric suction cup has likewise been described, in which the pressure detection unit detects the pressure between the suction cup and the component in real time and the vacuum pump automatically acts again when that pressure is lower than a second predetermined pressure [REF:CN-110630621-B].
10	
11	Other hand-carried powered suction devices have likewise been described. A cordless wand device for grasping objects such as silicon wafers has a housing with a hollow interior, a tip attached to the housing through a hollow tube and having a perimeter region contoured to form an airtight seal when placed against the surface of the object, a power source and a vacuum pump positioned within the housing, a switch by which the pump is turned on and off, and light-emitting diodes of different colours which indicate to an operator whether the power source is sufficiently charged to generate sufficient suction force to safely grasp the object, the sufficiency being determined from the voltage drop across a resistor network fed by the power source [REF:US-5374090-A]. What is indicated there is the state of the power source and the sufficiency of the suction force for taking hold, not how much hold remains on an object already being carried.
12	
13	A portable electric carrying suction cup structure has been described in which a handle is fixed to the upper end of a suction cup body and a vacuum pump is provided on the suction cup body, with a control unit connected between the pump and the power supply part, so that air is pumped out from between the suction cup body and the surface of a smooth material and is continuously pumped out after an airtight state has been reached in order to avoid loosening and falling during movement; the control unit is provided with a pressure gauge by which the user can know the pressure change, with a light source displaying different usage states, and with a buzzer for sending out alarm sounds according to different usage states [REF:CN-2806399-Y]. Here again the answer to a decaying grip is to keep the pump running, and what the buzzer is tied to is a usage state rather than the amount of grip left.
14	
15	A digital display suction cup has been described comprising a suction cup and a handle structure, the two ends of the handle structure carrying a switch button and a pressure relief valve, the handle structure carrying a battery and an electric vacuum pump connected to the suction cup through an air pipe, and the lower part of the battery end carrying an air pressure sensor and a display screen which displays the negative pressure value of the suction cup and the battery power, the battery being charged through a USB charging port [REF:US-2024424646-A1]. That device puts a number in front of the user and leaves the reading of the number, and the judgement of what it means for the panel in hand, to the user.
16	
17	A portable hand grab has been described including one or more suction cups, at least one handle connected to the suction cups, at least one electrical vacuum pump for at least partially evacuating a suction volume between the suction cups and the attachment surfaces, at least one vacuum sensor for detecting a vacuum level in the suction volume, a power storage unit, and an electronic controller configured to control the pump to evacuate the suction volume when the vacuum sensor detects the vacuum level being less than a preselected minimum vacuum level, together with an attach indicator which the controller activates when the vacuum sensor detects the vacuum level being greater than a preselected safe vacuum level [REF:WO-2017156581-A1]. The indicator there reports that attachment has been achieved, being activated above a preselected safe vacuum level, and the response to a vacuum level below the preselected minimum is once more to run the pump.
18	
19	A sucker for plate glass has also been described in which the sucker body defines a suction hole at its suction surface and carries a manually operated vacuum pump, a sensor communicating with the suction channel that connects the two suction holes and including a piston lever which moves in proportion to the degree of vacuum, a switch closed by the piston lever when the degree of vacuum reaches a predetermined value, a power source, and a sound generator which generates sound when the switch is closed [REF:US-5184858-A]. The pump in that sucker is worked by hand, and the sound is generated when the sensor detects a predetermined degree of vacuum, the passages of record describing that value only as a predetermined value.
20	
21	Multi-cup handling equipment has been described in which two or more vacuum modules are mounted on a mounting frame, each module having a cup, an electrically powered vacuum pump, a fluid circuit, a controller, and optionally a pressure sensor and a battery, with an interface through which a user selects an operational mode of the modules, and in which each module may include indicators that indicate a functional condition of the module visually or audibly [REF:WO-2022236379-A1].
22	
23	Two shortcomings persist for a person who is holding a panel in one hand. First, the response to a decaying grip in the known powered devices is to run the pump again: the device treats a falling vacuum as a housekeeping event to be corrected, and neither reference relates the low predetermined pressure at which it acts to the vacuum still needed to hold the load. If the leak is larger than the pump can make up - a torn lip, a dusty or porous panel, a cracked substrate - the pump simply runs while the grip continues to decay, and the user is told nothing until the panel is gone. Second, where a signal is given at all, it is given on a condition unrelated to the hold on the load (battery state or charge sufficiency), on a rate of change, on a usage state, on the achievement of attachment above a safe level, or at a preset or predetermined value whose relationship to the load-holding capacity of the cup is not established. None of these guarantees the one thing a person carrying a slab actually needs: notice that arrives while the cup is still holding, with grip left over to get the panel down.
24	
25	There remains a need for a self-contained, cordless, hand-held vacuum lifter that tells the user that the grip is failing at a point on the decay curve at which the grip has not yet failed.
26

A portable electric carrying suction cup structure has been described in which a handle is fixed to the upper end of a suction cup body and a vacuum pump is provided on the suction cup body, with a control unit connected between the pump and the power supply part, so that air is pumped out from between the suction cup body and the surface of a smooth material and is continuously pumped out after an airtight state has been reached in order to avoid loosening and falling during movement; the control unit is provided with a pressure gauge by which the user can know the pressure change, with a light source displaying different usage states, and with a buzzer for sending out alarm sounds according to different usage states [REF:CN-2806399-Y]. A digital display suction cup has been described comprising a suction cup and a handle structure, the two ends of the handle structure carrying a switch button and a pressure relief valve, the handle structure carrying a battery and an electric vacuum pump connected to the suction cup through an air pipe, and the lower part of the battery end carrying an air pressure sensor and a display screen which displays the negative pressure value of the suction cup and the battery power, the battery being charged through a USB charging port [REF:US-2024424646-A1]. That device puts a number in front of the user and leaves the reading of the number, and the judgement of what it means for the panel in hand, to the user.

A portable hand grab has been described including one or more suction cups, at least one handle connected to the suction cups, at least one electrical vacuum pump for at least partially evacuating a suction volume between the suction cups and the attachment surfaces, at least one vacuum sensor for detecting a vacuum level in the suction volume, a power storage unit, and an electronic controller configured to control the pump to evacuate the suction volume when the vacuum sensor detects the vacuum level being less than a preselected minimum vacuum level, together with an attach indicator which the controller activates when the vacuum sensor detects the vacuum level being greater than a preselected safe vacuum level [REF:WO-2017156581-A1]. The indicator there reports that attachment has been achieved, being activated above a preselected safe vacuum level, and the response to a vacuum level below the preselected minimum is once more to run the pump.

A sucker for plate glass has also been described in which the sucker body defines a suction hole at its suction surface and carries a manually operated vacuum pump, a sensor communicating with the suction channel that connects the two suction holes and including a piston lever which moves in proportion to the degree of vacuum, a switch closed by the piston lever when the degree of vacuum reaches a predetermined value, a power source, and a sound generator which generates sound when the switch is closed [REF:US-5184858-A]. The pump in that sucker is worked by hand, and the sound is generated when the sensor detects a predetermined degree of vacuum, the passages of record describing that value only as a predetermined value.

Multi-cup handling equipment has been described in which two or more vacuum modules are mounted on a mounting frame, each module having a cup, an electrically powered vacuum pump, a fluid circuit, a controller, and optionally a pressure sensor and a battery, with an interface through which a user selects an operational mode of the modules, and in which each module may include indicators that indicate a functional condition of the module visually or audibly [REF:WO-2022236379-A1].

Two shortcomings persist for a person who is holding a panel in one hand. First, the response to a decaying grip in the known powered devices is to run the pump again: the device treats a falling vacuum as a housekeeping event to be corrected, and neither reference relates the low predetermined pressure at which it acts to the vacuum still needed to hold the load. If the leak is larger than the pump can make up - a torn lip, a dusty or porous panel, a cracked substrate - the pump simply runs while the grip continues to decay, and the user is told nothing until the panel is gone. Second, where a signal is given at all, it is given on a condition unrelated to the hold on the load (battery state or charge sufficiency), on a rate of change, on a usage state, on the achievement of attachment above a safe level, or at a preset or predetermined value whose relationship to the load-holding capacity of the cup is not established. None of these guarantees the one thing a person carrying a slab actually needs: notice that arrives while the cup is still holding, with grip left over to get the panel down.

There remains a need for a self-contained, cordless, hand-held vacuum lifter that tells the user that the grip is failing at a point on the decay curve at which the grip has not yet failed.

3	A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is disclosed. The lifter has a rigid body comprising a handle, and a suction cup carried by the rigid body. Because the warning vacuum lies on the near side of the release vacuum, that interval exists by construction rather than by luck.

1	In the following description, reference is made to the accompanying drawings, which form a part hereof and in which are shown by way of illustration specific embodiments. Other embodiments may be used and structural changes may be made without departing from the scope of the disclosure. Like numerals refer to like parts throughout.
2	
3	FIG. 1 shows a cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 in use. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 comprises a rigid body 14 comprising a handle 16, and a suction cup 10 carried by the rigid body 14. The suction cup 10 comprises a flexible sealing lip 12. A workpiece 50, such as a glass pane or a stone slab, is gripped on its face by the suction cup 10 and is carried by the user by way of the handle 16.
4	
5	FIG. 2 is a vertical section through the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100, showing the suction cup 10, the flexible sealing lip 12, the rigid body 14, an electric vacuum pump 20, a port 22, a pressure sensor 30, a rechargeable battery 40, and the workpiece 50.
6	
7	The suction cup 10 carries the flexible sealing lip 12. The flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against the face of the workpiece 50 and closes the suction cup 10 against that face.
8	
9	The electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14. The electric vacuum pump 20 is configured to draw air through the port 22 so as to create a vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50. The pressure of the surrounding atmosphere acting on the outside of the suction cup 10 then clamps the suction cup 10, and with it the rigid body 14 and the handle 16, to the workpiece 50, so that a load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum. Running the electric vacuum pump 20 draws further air through the port 22 and increases the vacuum; air leaking back is a loss of vacuum and a weakening of the grip.
10	
11	The pressure sensor 30 is configured to monitor the vacuum. A warning indicator 32 is driven by the pressure sensor 30. The rechargeable battery 40 is configured to power the electric vacuum pump 20.
12	
13	FIG. 3 shows the arrangement schematically. The electric vacuum pump 20 draws air through the port 22 from between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50. The pressure sensor 30 monitors the vacuum so created and drives the warning indicator 32. The rechargeable battery 40 powers the electric vacuum pump 20.
14	
15	The warning function operates as follows. The electric vacuum pump 20 creates the vacuum, the user lifts and carries the workpiece 50, and the load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum. If the seal between the flexible sealing lip 12 and the workpiece 50 is imperfect, because of dust or grit under the lip, a textured or porous face, a damaged lip, or flexing of the workpiece 50, air bleeds back and the vacuum is progressively lost. From the point of view of the person holding the panel this loss is silent: nothing about the feel of the tool changes.
16	
17	Two vacuums are of interest during that loss. One is the release vacuum, the vacuum at which the suction cup 10 ceases to retain the load, that is, the vacuum at which the load can be dropped. The other is the warning vacuum, the vacuum at which the warning indicator 32 is driven to activate.
18	
19	The warning vacuum is fixed by reference to the release vacuum. It is the vacuum which is reached, as the vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50 is lost, before the release vacuum is reached. The warning indicator 32 accordingly activates at a moment when the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load, and the grip that remains between the warning vacuum and the release vacuum is a reserve. The warning indicator 32 is in this way configured to warn a user before the load can be dropped. During the interval that runs from the activation of the warning indicator 32 to the arrival of the vacuum at the release vacuum, the user still has a held load and a working grip. Nothing in the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 has to intervene and nothing has to be fast, because the reserve is what buys the time, and the reserve exists by construction from where the warning vacuum has been fixed.
20	
21	This is a different design decision from choosing a vacuum at which to run a pump again. A restart value is a value at which a pump is run again; it says nothing about how much grip is left, and a device that answers its crossing by running its pump will, when the leak is larger than the pump can make up, run the pump all the way past the release vacuum without ever telling the user that the grip is going. Fixing the warning vacuum by reference to the release vacuum instead is what gives the activation of the warning indicator 32 the meaning that the grip is failing and that the user still has hold of the panel. It is also a different decision from warning on how fast the vacuum is changing: a warning given on rate fires on a fast leak whatever grip is left, and stays quiet on a slow leak that has nonetheless eaten the whole reserve. And it is a different decision from reporting that attachment has been achieved, or that the battery is charged, or that a measured value can be read off a display, none of which tells a user carrying a slab how much of the hold is left.
22	
23	The distinction matters more for a hand-carried tool than for equipment on a frame or a boom. Frame-mounted and suspended lifters can be given their own remedies for a failing grip: a second vacuum source, a reservoir, an interlock that refuses further motion. A cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 has none of these. The only thing that can act on a failing grip is the person holding the handle 16, and a person needs to be told while there is still something to be done. Fixing the warning vacuum by reference to the release vacuum is what puts the warning inside the window in which the user can act.
24	
25	In embodiments, the workpiece 50 is a glass panel or a stone panel, the flexible sealing lip 12 being placed against a face of the panel. Such a panel is the workpiece 50 for which the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is principally intended.
26	
27	A method of lifting a workpiece 50 with the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is shown in FIG. 4. At a placing step 202, the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against a face of the workpiece 50. At an evacuating step 204, the electric vacuum pump 20, powered by the rechargeable battery 40, draws air through the port 22 and creates the vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50. At a carrying step 206, the workpiece 50 is lifted and a load is carried on the suction cup 10 by the handle 16, the load being retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum.
28	
29	At a monitoring step 208, the pressure sensor 30 monitors the vacuum while the load is retained. At an activating step 210, as the vacuum is lost, the pressure sensor 30 drives the warning indicator 32 to activate at the warning vacuum, which is reached before the release vacuum at which the suction cup 10 ceases to retain the load. The warning indicator 32 is therefore activated while the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load. Setting the workpiece 50 down while the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load is what the warning gives the user time to do, and the user, having been warned, sets the workpiece 50 down.
30	
31	The embodiments described above are illustrative rather than limiting. Features described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another unless the combination is technically impossible. Terms such as upper, lower, above, and below are used with reference to the orientation shown in the drawings and do not restrict the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 to any particular attitude in use. The scope of protection is defined by the claims.

The suction cup 10 comprises a flexible sealing lip 12. A workpiece 50, such as a glass pane or a stone slab, is gripped on its face by the suction cup 10 and is carried by the user by way of the handle 16.

FIG. 2 is a vertical section through the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100, showing the suction cup 10, the flexible sealing lip 12, the rigid body 14, an electric vacuum pump 20, a port 22, a pressure sensor 30, a rechargeable battery 40, and the workpiece 50.

The suction cup 10 carries the flexible sealing lip 12. The flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against the face of the workpiece 50 and closes the suction cup 10 against that face.

The electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14. The electric vacuum pump 20 is configured to draw air through the port 22 so as to create a vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50. The pressure of the surrounding atmosphere acting on the outside of the suction cup 10 then clamps the suction cup 10, and with it the rigid body 14 and the handle 16, to the workpiece 50, so that a load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum. Running the electric vacuum pump 20 draws further air through the port 22 and increases the vacuum; air leaking back is a loss of vacuum and a weakening of the grip.

The pressure sensor 30 is configured to monitor the vacuum. A warning indicator 32 is driven by the pressure sensor 30. The rechargeable battery 40 is configured to power the electric vacuum pump 20.

FIG. 3 shows the arrangement schematically. The electric vacuum pump 20 draws air through the port 22 from between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50. The pressure sensor 30 monitors the vacuum so created and drives the warning indicator 32. The rechargeable battery 40 powers the electric vacuum pump 20.

The warning function operates as follows. The electric vacuum pump 20 creates the vacuum, the user lifts and carries the workpiece 50, and the load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum. If the seal between the flexible sealing lip 12 and the workpiece 50 is imperfect, because of dust or grit under the lip, a textured or porous face, a damaged lip, or flexing of the workpiece 50, air bleeds back and the vacuum is progressively lost. From the point of view of the person holding the panel this loss is silent: nothing about the feel of the tool changes.

Two vacuums are of interest during that loss. One is the release vacuum, the vacuum at which the suction cup 10 ceases to retain the load, that is, the vacuum at which the load can be dropped. The other is the warning vacuum, the vacuum at which the warning indicator 32 is driven to activate.

The warning vacuum is fixed by reference to the release vacuum. It is the vacuum which is reached, as the vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50 is lost, before the release vacuum is reached. The warning indicator 32 accordingly activates at a moment when the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load, and the grip that remains between the warning vacuum and the release vacuum is a reserve. The warning indicator 32 is in this way configured to warn a user before the load can be dropped. During the interval that runs from the activation of the warning indicator 32 to the arrival of the vacuum at the release vacuum, the user still has a held load and a working grip. Nothing in the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 has to intervene and nothing has to be fast, because the reserve is what buys the time, and the reserve exists by construction from where the warning vacuum has been fixed.

This is a different design decision from choosing a vacuum at which to run a pump again. A restart value is a value at which a pump is run again; it says nothing about how much grip is left, and a device that answers its crossing by running its pump will, when the leak is larger than the pump can make up, run the pump all the way past the release vacuum without ever telling the user that the grip is going. Fixing the warning vacuum by reference to the release vacuum instead is what gives the activation of the warning indicator 32 the meaning that the grip is failing and that the user still has hold of the panel. It is also a different decision from warning on how fast the vacuum is changing: a warning given on rate fires on a fast leak whatever grip is left, and stays quiet on a slow leak that has nonetheless eaten the whole reserve. And it is a different decision from reporting that attachment has been achieved, or that the battery is charged, or that a measured value can be read off a display, none of which tells a user carrying a slab how much of the hold is left.

The distinction matters more for a hand-carried tool than for equipment on a frame or a boom. Frame-mounted and suspended lifters can be given their own remedies for a failing grip: a second vacuum source, a reservoir, an interlock that refuses further motion. A cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 has none of these. The only thing that can act on a failing grip is the person holding the handle 16, and a person needs to be told while there is still something to be done. Fixing the warning vacuum by reference to the release vacuum is what puts the warning inside the window in which the user can act.

In embodiments, the workpiece 50 is a glass panel or a stone panel, the flexible sealing lip 12 being placed against a face of the panel. Such a panel is the workpiece 50 for which the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is principally intended.

A method of lifting a workpiece 50 with the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is shown in FIG. 4. At a placing step 202, the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against a face of the workpiece 50. At an evacuating step 204, the electric vacuum pump 20, powered by the rechargeable battery 40, draws air through the port 22 and creates the vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50. At a carrying step 206, the workpiece 50 is lifted and a load is carried on the suction cup 10 by the handle 16, the load being retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum.

At a monitoring step 208, the pressure sensor 30 monitors the vacuum while the load is retained. At an activating step 210, as the vacuum is lost, the pressure sensor 30 drives the warning indicator 32 to activate at the warning vacuum, which is reached before the release vacuum at which the suction cup 10 ceases to retain the load. The warning indicator 32 is therefore activated while the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load. Setting the workpiece 50 down while the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load is what the warning gives the user time to do, and the user, having been warned, sets the workpiece 50 down.

13	Abstract: The invention concerns a vacuum lifter to transport loads with an adhesion surface and comprises at least one suction head with at least one projecting annular seal on its suction side, where the vacuum chamber(s) enclosed by the annular seal(s) is (are) hooked up to a main vacuum source and where additionally a battery-fed emergency vacuum source is provided which can be started by an emergency switch. In order to avert as much as possible crashes when using such a vacuum lifter, a pressure pickup (67) is associated with the or at least one of the vacuum chambers (13) and is coupled in such a way with a malfunction alarm (69) that when a preset limit pressure is exceeded during vacuum operation, the malfunction alarm (69) shall be turned ON.
14	Claims: A vacuum lifter, comprising: a) a suction plate assembly; b) at least first and second seals projecting from sid assembly and defining therebetween a vacuum chamber; c) a main vacuum source operatively associated with said assembly for applying a vacuum to said vacuum chamber; d) an emergency vacuum source operatively associated with said assembly for selectively applying a vacuum to said vacuum chamber, said emergency vacuum source being electrically operable during application of the vacuum thereof; e) means operatively associated with said vacuum chamber for monitoring the vacuum therein; and f) means operatively associated with said monitoring means and with said emergency vacuum source for causing automatic electrical operation of said emergency vacuum source when said monitoring means detects in said vacuum chamber a vacuum pressure less than a preselected limit. The lifter of claim 1, wherein: a) said monitoring means includes a pressure pickup. The lifter of claim 1, wherein: a) said causing means includes a remotely operable switch. The lifter of claim 1, wherein: a) said causing means includes means for permitting operation of said emergency vacuum source when the vacuum in said vacuum chamber is less than said preselected limit so that said main and emergency vacuum sources may operate simultaneously for thereby causing the vacuum in said vacuum chamber to be twice the vacuum applied solely by said main vacuum source. The lifter of claim 1, wherein: a) said emergency vacuum source includes a battery for assuring operation thereof. The lifter of claim 1, wherein: a) each of said seals is resilient. The lifter of claim 1, wherein said assembly includes: a) a vacuum vessel comprising a closed body having a top plate and a bottom plate; b) each of said seals extends from said bottom plate; c) said main and emergency vacuum sources apply a vacuum to the interior of said vessel; and d) means extend from the interior of said vessel to said vacuum chamber for applying the vacuum in said vessel 6 to said vacuum chamber. The lifter of claim 7, wherein: a) said applying means includes a valve assembly for controlling the application of vacuum to said vacuum chamber so that said vacuum chamber may be vented to atmosphere without venting said vessel. The lifter of claim 8, wherein: a) said valve assembly includes a three way valve and a check valve. The lifter of claim 7, wherein: a) said applying means includes a through pipe extending through said vessel and communicating with said chamber; and b) a vacuum pipe extends from the interior of said vessel and communicates with said through pipe. The lifter in claim 7, wherein: a) a central pipe extends between said plates; and b) an aperture in said bottom plate is aligned with said central pipe so that said central pipe is open to the atmosphere. A vacuum lifter, comprising: a) a vacuum vessel comprising upper and lower plates and a peripheral wall extending therebetween; b) at least first and second resilient seals extending from and about said lower plate for defining therebetween a vacuum chamber; c) a main vacuum source and an emergency vacuum source, each of said sources communicating with the interior of said vessel for applying a vacuum thereto, wherein said emergency vacuum source is electrically operable during application of the vacuum thereof; d) a measurement pick-up operatively associated with said vessel for monitoring the vacuum therein; e) a vacuum supply extending between said vessel and said chamber for causing the vacuum inside said vessel to be selectively applied to said chamber; and f) control means operatively associated with said emergency vacuum source and said pick-up for causing automatic electrical operation of said emergency vacuum source when said monitoring means detects in said vacuum chamber a vacuum pressure less than a preselected limit. The lifter of claim 12, wherein said vacuum supply system includes: a) an aperture in said upper plate; b) a through pipe extending through said vessel and communicating with said chamber; and c) a vacuum pipe interconnecting said aperture and said through pipe. The lifter of claim 13, wherein: a) a valve assembly is interposed in said vacuum pipe for permitting said through pipe and thereby said chamber to vent to atmosphere while maintaining the vacuum in said vessel. The lifter of claim 12, wherein: a) said control means includes a remotely operable switch for causing operation of said emergency vacuum source. The lifter of claim 15, wherein: a) said switch is operable when the vacuum in said vessel is less than said preselected limit so that said main and emergency vacuum sources may operate simultaneously. The lifter of claim 12, wherein: a) said emergency vacuum source includes an electrically operable motor; and b) a battery is operably associated with said motor for assuring operation thereof. The lifter of claim 12, wherein: a) each of said seals is resilient.

13	Abstract: An electric sucker comprises a body, a vacuum pump, a pressure sensing unit and a start key. When the user presses the activation key, the vacuum pump will act to pump out the air between the electric sucker and the component attached to the electric sucker, so that the electric sucker is adsorbed on the component. The pressure sensing unit can detect the pressure between the electric sucker and the component in real time. When the pressure sensing unit detects that the pressure between the electric suction cup and the component is lower than a second preset pressure, the vacuum pump automatically acts to pump out the air between the electric suction cup and the component again. After the user sets up the electric chuck on the component that wants to adsorb, can make the electric chuck adsorb automatically on simply through pressing the start key on the component. Then, the electric suction cup can automatically detect the pressure between the electric suction cup and the component in real time, and automatically perform air suction again when the pressure is lower than a second preset pressure, so that the safety of related personnel using the electric suction cup can be ensured.
